extracted.intended_audience: researchers, academic librarians, journal editors, publishers, and policy-makers concerned with identifying and evaluating predatory journals and lists
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic evaluation of lists/databases that identify predatory journals and publishers, focusing on their governance, methods, transparency, criteria, and update practices to assess reliability and usefulness for researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment year / temporal origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The year the list was established (temporal origin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess recency and historical context; e.g., six (60.0%) of identified lists were established after 2017. Table 1 lists temporal origins for each list (e.g., Beall’s List 2008, Kscien’s List 2020).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible entity / institutional oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Who created/maintains the list (independent scholar, commercial entity, governmental body, research organization, academic institution, nonprofit, unknown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important for assessing conflicts of interest, resources, and accountability (e.g., Cabell’s = commercial entity; Kanalregister = governmental body; Kscien = research organization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative framework (centralized/decentralized/collaborative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The governance/administration model used to run the list (centralized, decentralized, collaborative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May affect consistency and update mechanisms; seven (63.6%) operated centralized, three (27.3%) decentralized, one (9.1%) collaborative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility (public vs subscription-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list is freely publicly accessible or requires subscription/payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impacts equity of access and utility for researchers; nine (90.0%) were public while one (10.0%) was subscription-based (Cabell’s), raising concerns about barriers for low-resource researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content coverage (journals, publishers, hijacked journals, conferences, misleading metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of entities included on the list (predatory publishers, predatory standalone journals, hijacked journals, misleading metrics, predatory conferences, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determines breadth of protection offered; e.g., many lists cover both journals and publishers, Kscien expanded to include conferences and a cumulative list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of publishers and number of journals listed
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative counts of publishers and journals included on the list (numerical coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a descriptive metric of list size/coverage (medians and ranges reported; e.g., median publishers 1362, journals 1489). Large counts may indicate comprehensiveness but could reflect differing inclusion thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data format (database, simple webpage, PDF)
rubrics_metrics.description: The file or presentation format in which the list is provided (database, simple webpage, PDF file).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affects usability, searchability, and ability to integrate with tools; six (60.0%) used databases, three (30.0%) simple webpages, one (10.0%) a PDF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating date / updating frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of last update and stated frequency of updates (daily, monthly, annually, not specified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical for reliability given rapid emergence of predatory journals; only one list was updated daily, two annually, one monthly, six did not specify frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of updating (last update documented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list documents last update dates and makes update practices transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of update transparency can mislead users; the review highlights inconsistent documentation of update practices across lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of identification (manual review, external reports, stinging operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: How items are identified for listing: manual review by curators, external community reports, or active sting operations testing journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most lists (90.0%) relied on manual review and external reports; only one (Kscien) used a sting operation as part of identification. Presence of sting operations provides empirical evidence of poor peer review but is rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and specificity of identification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list specifies explicit criteria (and how many/what type) used to label an entity predatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only four (40.0%) lists had specified criteria. Example: Cabell’s published 74 criteria (v1.1). Specified, structured criteria increase objectivity; unspecified criteria reduce transparency and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity vs subjectivity of listing criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the criteria are objective, measurable, and reproducible versus subjective judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beall’s List was criticized for subjective judgments; lists with clear, objective itemized criteria (e.g., Cabell’s) are preferred to reduce bias and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of adding items / inclusion process
rubrics_metrics.description: The documented process by which items are added to the list (manual review protocols, community submissions, automated detection, unspecified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nine (90.0%) used manual review; robust documented inclusion processes improve trustworthiness. Lack of documentation weakens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delisting criteria and appeal process
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list documents clear criteria and procedures for removing items and provides an appeals or remediation pathway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delisting criteria were poorly documented in eight (80.0%) lists; only one list provided clearly defined delisting criteria. Transparent delisting and appeal mechanisms reduce risk of permanent reputational harm and legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting criteria / changes in criteria over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list updates or adapts its criteria to respond to evolving predatory tactics and whether changes are documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapting criteria is necessary as predatory publishers become more sophisticated (e.g., fabrication of archives, securing indexing). Documentation of criteria changes supports accountability and historical tracing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical tracking and cumulative records
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list maintains history of entries/changes (historical tracking) and cumulative documentation of journals associated with predatory publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kscien introduced a Cumulative List to document affiliated journals systematically. Historical tracking aids research, transparency, and understanding of trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community involvement / reporting mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the list solicits or incorporates community feedback, reports, or crowdsourced inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community involvement can enhance detection but requires moderation to avoid abuse; Cabell’s and some others allow community reports. Lack of community mechanisms may limit responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary source attribution / provenance (use of Beall’s List or others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list cites primary sources or relies on previous lists (e.g., Beall’s List) as part of its evidence base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beall’s List was cited as a primary source by 40.0% of lists. Reliance on prior lists requires scrutiny for propagation of original biases or errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability and documented remediation (appeal process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and clarity of an appeals or remediation process for entities seeking removal or correction on the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned in Table 3 as an important documentation practice (some lists record appeal processes; others do not). Clear appeals reduce legal risk and support fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of methodology and decision-making processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list publishes its methods, decision rules, reviewer qualifications, committees, and internal governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological transparency (who reviews, how decisions made) is essential for trust; the review excluded lists lacking detailed criteria or governance transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating/maintenance resources and sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: the resources and organizational capacity to sustain timely updates and governance (commercial vs nonprofit vs individual maintenance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subscription/commercial models (e.g., Cabell’s) may have more resources but restrict access; individual/anonymous maintenance (Beall’s original) may face sustainability and legal risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusivity and equity of access
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list’s accessibility model (public vs subscription) enables researchers globally, including low- and middle-income countries, to use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subscription-only models may exacerbate inequalities; the review flags access barriers as a concern for utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical testing (stings) as validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list uses empirical tests (stinging operations) to validate predatory practices (e.g., lack of peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bohannon’s sting illustrated the method’s ability to reveal peer-review failures. Only one list in the review incorporated a sting; empirical testing strengthens evidence but raises ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity of classification (categories and taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of categorical detail used to classify entities (e.g., suspicious publishers, predatory standalone journals, hijacked journals, falsified metrics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beall’s four-category taxonomy exemplifies granular classification; finer taxonomies help users understand types of harm and appropriate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity around what counts as predatory (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the list provides a clear operational definition of 'predatory publishing' and explicit inclusion/exclusion boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of a universal definition complicates listing; the review emphasizes that absence of standardized criteria reduces reliability and leads to inconsistent identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of statistical and descriptive metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision of descriptive statistics and metadata about the list (medians, ranges, counts, update logs) to inform users about scope and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review reports medians and ranges for publisher and journal counts and tabulates administrative characteristics; such metadata helps users evaluate list coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk management and defensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: whether the list’s processes and documentation mitigate legal risk (e.g., to withstand challenges by listed publishers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beall’s List faced legal challenges and was taken down; structured criteria, documented processes, and appeal pathways improve legal defensibility.
